newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Archaic Indian laws out of tune with times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Archaic Indian laws out of tune with times.

text.p: The prudish spirit of India's former empress, Britain's Queen Victoria, lives on, embodied in Section 377 of India's Penal Code.
Homosexuality and oral sex are banned, considered as "unnatural" as sexual activity with animals.
Depressed? Try committing suicide in India and you could go to prison.
Accepting a bribe is not considered corruption unless taken by a government servant.
And if you have second thoughts hijacking an aircraft, there is no law under which you can be prosecuted -- hijacking is a crime but attempted hijacking is not.

Hotels and cafes are required by a law enacted in 1887 to serve water free to all passers-by in a tropical country where water now sells for 13 rupees (36 cents) a bottle and the mineral water market is estimated at about one billion rupees.
And nearly 50 years after the constitution declared them equal to men, a woman still cannot be the legal guardian of her child until a court declares her fit.
Absurd? The Indian government seems to think so too.
ANTIQUATED LAWS AND THE RIGHT TO INFORMATION
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has vowed to overhaul some 1,500 irrelevant laws, some of which were written in the 19th century.
Some regulations still refer to Queen Victoria, who ruled over India when it was part of British empire. Half a century has passed since India won freedom from colonial rule.

"The effective delivery of services and benefits under various welfare schemes to the public is frustrated by rigid procedures and archaic laws, apart from the insensitive attitude of the officials and the unwarranted transaction costs," the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances recently admitted.
The department is working closely with a panel of legal experts charged with reviewing India's 6,500 federal and state laws.
Social activist H.D. Shourie is working on a parallel government project -- providing 930 million people with the right to information.

"Our government's functioning is on the basis of the colonial era, with the result that it is enshrouded in secrecy and that unfortunately leads to malfunctioning and corruption," Shourie told Reuters.
Shourie, who leads a public interest group called Common Cause, also heads a committee that has asked the government to enact a Freedom of Information Bill.
"Every individual must have the right to ask for information about the functioning of the government," Shourie said.

"Every day Common Cause gets complaints -- consumers want to know on what basis they are being charged for telephone calls and electricity. You can run from pillar to post trying to find out but everyone refers you elsewhere and you will never, ever find out," Shourie said.
COMPLEX WEB OF RELIGIOUS LAWS

Law in India, a country as large as most of Europe, is further complicated by separate regulations for each of its religious groups -- Hindus, Moslems, Parsis, Christians and other communities are each covered by different civil laws.
These complex distinctions are a sensitive legal area that the government dare not touch for fear of offending religious leaders, who fiercely defend their right to be different.
And so, Hindu women still cannot ask for ancestral property to be divided so that they get a separate share.
Parsi women have no right of adoption independent of their husbands. Parsis are also forbidden to adopt children outside their faith.
Constitutionally secular but mostly Hindu India has the world's second largest population of Moslems, whose civil law is drawn mainly from the Koran and the Prophet Mohammad's sayings.
A Moslem can divorce his wife merely by uttering the word "talaq", or divorce, three times in front of two witnesses.
Moslem women were granted the right to seek divorce in 1939, but a Moslem woman's share in ancestral inheritance is still half of her brother's.
"You can name any man on the street as your child's guardian, even though as a woman you cannot be the guardian under law," says Health Minister Renuka Chowdhury.

Most forms in India ask the applicant to fill in their father's name -- unless the applicant is a married woman, in which case she is supposed to write her husband's name. The Sanskrit word for husband, "pati," means owner.

It is considered disrespectful for a woman to utter her husband's name, and Election Commission officials say their reluctance to provide that vital detail is the reason why many women are not included on voters lists.
Lawyer Sona Khan, who in 1986 won a landmark ruling that granted Moslem women the right to maintenance, says Indian laws still have a tenuous link with justice.
"We borrowed the judicial system from the colonial power," she says. "It was meant to administer a colony. And a woman was never expected to be a earning member. She was meant only to be protected."
